questions.solution_html:

  • economic variables- When monetary policy changes are anticipated, individuals adjust
  • their behavior, making the po licy ineffective in changing real output or employment -
  • Thus, in the long run, money becomes neutral, it only affects nominal variable(such as
  • prices and wages), not real variables.

questions.question: Differentiate between commodity money, fiat money, and representative money with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Commodity Money: Has intrinsic value (value in itself)-Used historically as gold,
  • silver, salt, or cattle-Example: Gold coins in ancient trade.
  • Fiat Money: Has no intrinsic value; its value comes from government decree-Backed
  • by trust in the issuing authority-Example: Indian Rupee, US Dollar.
  • Representative Money: Paper or token representing a claim on a commodity that can
  • be redeemed-Convertible into gold or silver during the gold standard era-Example:
  • Gold certificates or paper backed by gold reserves.

questions.question: Explain the quantity theory of money / [CO2, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• The Quantity Theory of Money explains the relationship between money supply and
  • price level- There are two major versions of quantity theory of money-Cash Transaction
  • Approach and Cash Balance Approach-Cash Transaction Approach: Fisher- medium of
  • exchange as the major functions of money- Fisher’s Equation of Exchange MV=PT.
  • where,
  • M = Total supply of money
  • V = Velocity of circulation of money
  • P = General price level
  • T = Total transactions in physical goods
  • V and T are constant in the short run- Any change in M leads to a proportional change
  • in P.-An increase in money supply causes inflation; reduction leads to deflation.
  • Cambridge Cash Balance Approach: Popu larised by Pigou, Marshall, Robertson,
  • Keynes and Hawtrey. -Emphasizes store of value function of money or cash balance
  • instead of transactions.
  • Pigou’s Equation:- π =KR/M
  • Where,
  • Π – The Purchasing power of money
  • K- The proportion of income that people like to hold in the form of money
  • R- The volume of real income
  • M- The stock of supply of money in the country at a given time
  • It shows that the purchasing power of money or the value of money (π) varies directly
  • with K or R, and inversely with M.
  • Marshallian Cash Balance Equation:- M=KPY
  • M- Supply of money
  • P- Price level
  • Y- Aggregate real income
  • 25900347
  • K- Fraction of the real income which the people desire to hold in the form of money.
  • P is directly related to the M and inversely related to the KY
  • Robertson’s Equation:- M=KPT
  • P changes directly with M and inversely with K and T
  • Keyne’s Reformulated Quantity Theory of Money: n=pk
  • Keynes Demand for Money- criticism against classical quantity theory.

questions.question: How do macroeconomic factors such as inflation expectations and uncertainty affect the liquidity of financial markets / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Inflation Expectations: When inflation is expected to rise, inte rest rates increase -
  • Investors shift from bonds to real assets, reducing liquidity in financial markets.
  • Uncertainty: Political or economic uncertainty causes investors to hoard cash-V olatility
  • increases and market confidence decreases, lowering liquidity.
  • Interest Rate Fluctuations: Higher rates discourage borrowing and reduce trading
  • volumes.
  • Exchange Rate V olatility: Depreciating currency may cause foreign investors to
  • withdraw funds, shrinking liquidity.
  • Economic Growth Prospects: Stable and positive growth enhances liquidity as investors
  • are confident.
  • Liquidity is sensitive to macroeconomic conditions- stable inflation and low uncertainty
  • support active, liquid financial markets.

questions.question: Distinguish between 'Tier 1 Capital' and 'Tier 2 Capital' / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Tier 1 Capital:- Core capital that provides permanent equity and absorbs losses without
  • ceasing operations-Components:- Paid-up equity capital, disclosed reserves, retained
  • earnings- Risk Absorption:-Stronger, first line of defense.- Regulatory Requirement:-
  • Minimum 6% of risk-weighted assets- Example:-Common equity, stock surplus.
  • Tier 2 Capital:- Supplementary capital that absorbs losses only in case of liquidation -
  • Components:- Undisclosed reserves, subordinated debt, hybrid instruments - Risk
  • Absorption:- Weaker; second line of defense- Regulatory Requirement:- Maximum 2%
  • of risk-weighted assets- Example:- Subordinated term debt, revaluation reserves.
  • Tier 1 ensures financial strength and solvency; Tier 2 provides additional protection in
  • adverse conditions.

questions.question: Discuss factors such as variable time lags, financial market imperfections, and the presence of a "liquidity trap" that can impede the effectiveness of monetary policy. / [CO1, CO2, CO3, CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Variable Time Lags: Policy changes take time to affect output and prices-Recognition,
  • implementation, and impact lags reduce policy precision.
  • Financial Market Imperfections: Underdeveloped markets, credit constraints, or weak
  • transmission channels distort the effect of interest rate changes.
  • Liquidity Trap: When interest rates are near zero, people prefer to hold cash rather than
  • bonds-Monetary expansion fails to stimulate investment or spending.
  • Expectations and Confidence: If people expect future inflation or instability, monetary
  • easing may fail to boost demand.
  • External Factors: Capital flows and exchange rate pressures can offset domestic policy
  • actions.
  • Due to these structural and behavioral factors, monetary policy may lose its
  • effectiveness, particularly during recessions or unstable conditions.

questions.question: How does money act as a solution to the problems of barter? Explain with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Barter system faced major difficulties: Double coincidence of wants,Lack of common
  • measure of value,Indivisibility of goods, Difficulty in storing wealth and Lack of
  • deferred payments.
  • Money solves these problems:-
  • Medium of Exchange: Eliminates double coincidence of want s. Example: Buying
  • clothes with cash instead of exchanging goods.
  • Measure of Value: Common unit for pricing-the rupee.
  • Store of Value: Money retains value for future use.
  • Standard of Deferred Payment: Future payments can be expressed in money.
  • Transfer of Value: Easy transfer from one person to another.
  • Money enhances efficiency and expands trade by replacing the inefficient barter
  • system.
